deep.reconstruction:
This page has no derivations, formulas or computations. It is a set of aphoristic, philosophical notes that continue the previous page's remarks on mathematics, physics and the axiomatic method. Item by item:

(1) Between thinking (Denken) and happening (Geschehen) there is no difference of principle and no qualitative difference. Hilbert offers this as the explanation of the 'pre-established harmony' and of the fact that simple experimental laws always allow simple theories. This theme returns on the next page as a 'philosophical problem' whose deeper ground is to be found.

(2) A programmatic task: 'Prove the following theorem: if an existence proof has been given in mathematics, then the decision (by a finite number of steps, as one says) whether ... is always possible.' The image reads 'Entscheidung' (decision), not 'Construktion'. The '...' is left blank by Hilbert. Read literally as a metamathematical statement, it would say: (a classical proof that some x exists with P(x)) implies (a finite procedure deciding the relevant question, or exhibiting x). This is a programme statement, not a proof. It belongs with Hilbert's 'no ignorabimus' conviction and the next page's 'Beweis aller Beweise: dass man den Beweis immer muss finden können'.

(3) Physics speculation. Our grandchildren will laugh that we still had to wind our watches every evening instead of letting heat turn into work. He asks whether living beings in nature use a perpetuum mobile of the second kind, remarking that 'submicrobes' are small enough for it. This is the Maxwell-demon idea: microscopic agents exploiting fluctuations to violate the second law.

(4) Not all human knowledge is yet ripe for mathematics. But only in mathematics does human thought find its definitive and fixed expression; this is where the hard struggle for clarity takes place. He cites Kant's fundamental question: 'How is pure mathematics possible?'

(5) Scientific education should enable everyone to turn any confused, wild, loose thought into a mathematical theorem. That is the axiomatic method, which first creates the fixed steps, like a glacier guide, without which progress is impossible.

(6) A sentence that continues onto the next page: 'Whoever today still sticks only to experiments, e.g. that three support points fix a plane, or that bodies can rotate, and accordingly only ...'. This continues the previous page's polemic against doing geometry while ignoring modern physics.
errors: Item (2), read literally as a theorem ('every existence proof yields a finite decision or construction procedure'), is false in general. The halting set is definable and the corresponding existence claims are classically provable, yet it is undecidable (Turing 1936, Church 1936). The Entscheidungsproblem for first-order logic was shown unsolvable in 1936. Gödel 1931 also undermines the related 'every question decidable' conviction. Hilbert records it here as a desideratum to be proved, not as a proven result.

Item (3), using living microbes as a perpetuum mobile of the second kind, is physically untenable. Szilard (1929) and later Landauer/Bennett showed that measurement and memory-erasure costs save the second law for Maxwell-demon-type agents. Smoluchowski (1912) had already argued that automatic demons fail because of their own fluctuations.
Item (1), that simple experimental laws 'always' permit simple theories, is a philosophical assertion, not a demonstrable claim.

results.what: Programme: every mathematical existence proof should be convertible into a finite decision/construction procedure ('Beweise den folgenden Satz ...')
results.modern_name: Decidability / constructivity programme; precursor of the Entscheidungsproblem and of Hilbert's finitist programme ('no ignorabimus')
results.usually_credited_to: Hilbert (Paris problems 1900, 'no ignorabimus'; Entscheidungsproblem formulated by Hilbert-Ackermann 1928); refuted by Gödel 1931 and Church/Turing 1936

results.what: Speculation that microscopic living organisms might realize a perpetuum mobile of the second kind
Pre-established harmony between thought and reality; simplicity of laws implies simplicity of theories
results.modern_name: Pre-established harmony between mathematics and physics (cf. Wigner's 'unreasonable effectiveness')
results.usually_credited_to: Leibniz (term); Hilbert and Minkowski in Göttingen usage; Wigner 1960

results.what: Axiomatic method as the means of turning any loose thought into a mathematical theorem; Kant's question 'Wie ist reine Mathematik möglich?'

deep.surprise_reason: These are philosophical jottings that closely match Hilbert's well-known public views: no ignorabimus, the axiomatic method, pre-established harmony, and the Kant reference. The explicit wish to prove 'existence proof implies a finite decision procedure' is a nice private formulation anticipating the Entscheidungsproblem. Its spirit is well documented as Hilbert's, though, and the Maxwell-demon speculation about microbes was common in contemporary discussion (e.g. Smoluchowski). There is no new mathematics on the page.

checkable.asserts: Three non-collinear points (0,0,0), (1,0,0), (0,1,0) fix a unique plane. The determinant equals -z (up to sign), so the plane through them is z=0. This illustrates the 'three support points determine the plane' remark.
This determinant is identically 0. Collinear points do not fix a plane, so the 'three points' fact needs non-collinearity.
